Doing Better at Doing Good: Lessons from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis After 20 Years of Poverty 
Graduation Programs
Samantha Carter, Edward Jee, Dean Karlan, and Patrick Premand
NBER Working Paper No. 35991
November 2026
JEL No. C11, D61, H53, I32, I38, O12, O13
ABSTRACT
Multifaceted poverty Graduation programs that aim to increase income generating activities for 
low-income households are being rapidly adopted and scaled by nonprofit organizations and 
governments. This paper conducts a Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis of 49 studies 
(encompassing 81 treatment variations) on poverty Graduation programs, defined as containing at 
least three of five components: consumption support, savings facilitation, skills training, coaching, 
and a lumpsum transfer. The analysis finds large gains across economic and psychosocial 
outcomes: monthly consumption rises by 38 USD PPP (11 percent), income by 28 USD PPP (15 
percent), alongside improvements in savings, assets, food security, mental health, and women’s 
empowerment. Beyond these average treatment effects, three results stand out. First, programs with 
large transfers (at least 400 USD PPP) have larger treatment effects but are not more cost-effective. 
Second, more expensive programs generate larger treatment effects, but the improvements are not 
commensurate with the cost increases; thus, lower cost programs tend to be more cost-effective. 
Third, programs implemented from 2016 onward perform considerably better than those 
implemented prior to 2016: benefit-cost ratios from 2016 onward are 5.39, compared to 2.89 
through 2015. Neither changes in cost nor in high-level design (components) explain this upward 
trend. Considering other heavily studied interventions, the results show a similar upward trend for 
treatment effects on behavior change from financial education but not for unconditional cash 
transfers. The paper hypothesizes a mechanism of continuous sector-community learning and 
improved implementation quality.
Samantha Carter
Livelihood Impact Fund
samanthaw.carter@gmail.com
Edward Jee
The University of Chicago
edjee@uchicago.edu
Dean Karlan
Northwestern University
and NBER
dean.karlan@gmail.com
Patrick Premand
The World Bank
ppremand@worldbank.org
1 Introduction
Graduation programs aim to generate long-run socioeconomic impacts by helping low-income house-
holds engage in new or expanded income generating activities. Under the premise that market frictions
are not single-faceted, the programs deliver a package of components, specifically some combination of
consumption support, savings facilitation, skills training, coaching and an asset transfer or a lump-sum
cash grant.
Tests of an initial design by BRAC in Bangladesh (Bandiera et al., 2017) and seven coordinated
adaptations in Ethiopia, Ghana, Honduras, India, Pakistan, Peru, and the Republic of Yemen (Baner-
jee et al., 2015a; Brune et al., 2022) led to an initial “proof of concept” of the Graduation model.
Economic inclusion programs, including Graduation approaches, have been further adopted, adapted
and scaled by nonprofit organizations and governments in 88 countries, reaching over 70 million in-
dividuals (Ar´ evalo-S´ anchez et al., 2024). In the process, implementers have experimented with both
simpler and more complicated versions, while also pushing to find ways to deliver programs at a lower
unit cost without sacrificing treatment effects. The rapid spread of poverty Graduation programs,
often also considered within a broader set of “economic inclusion” programs that may not include
all core components, has been accompanied by a robust research agenda, testing everything from al-
ternative bundles of components to tailoring for particular populations to varying scale and delivery
approaches. With 41 journal articles, reports, and working papers covering randomized evaluations of
the Graduation model, we can now begin to quantitatively aggregate results and examine questions
about optimal design and trends in the practice and impact of these programs.
We conduct a meta-analysis of multi-faceted programs that include at least three of the five core
Graduation program components: (i) consumption support, (ii) training, (iii) coaching, (iv) savings
facilitation or encouragement of savings, and (v) an asset or lump sum cash grants. We therefore
cover both “core” Graduation programs, as initially implemented by NGOs such as BRAC, as well
as a broader set of “economic inclusion” programs which are inspired by the Graduation model and
keep its multifaceted logic, but are, in some cases, lighter in scope. This inclusion criterion reflects
the heterogeneity of programs now operating around the world (Ar´ evalo-S´ anchez et al., 2024), while
maintaining sufficient conceptual coherence to permit meaningful pooling. In total, the meta-analysis
draws on 49 study records from 41 publications, reports, and working papers, covering 40 unique
randomizations. These contain 81 reported treatment variations and 123 treatment-variation-wave
observations; consolidating repeated reports of the same intervention lineage yields 68 unique treatment
arms and 109 canonical treatment-arm-wave observations.
We build on two recently conducted meta-analyses that encompass Graduation programs. Kondylis
and Loeser (2021) examine the persistence of consumption impacts for 17 RCTs, comparing Graduation
programs to unconditional cash transfers. Results support the idea that Graduation programs address
constraints beyond mere liquidity: Graduation programs generate more persistent impacts, but are less
cost-effective in the short run and show more heterogeneous impacts – which plausibly reflects their
2
increased complexity. Leight et al. (2024), casting a wider net by including non-randomized studies
as well as “cash-plus” interventions (which include Graduation studies but also studies with only one
added component beyond cash), examines 104 studies and impacts focused on consumption, income
and labor supply. They find larger effects for “cash-plus” interventions than mere cash, as well as
higher cost-effectiveness under some assumptions. 1
We differentiate from these meta-analyses on four dimensions. First, we focus on Graduation pro-
grams, including neither unconditional cash transfers nor “cash-plus” interventions that have only one
additional component beyond cash. 2 Second, beyond documenting gains on monthly consumption (by
38 USD PPP, or 11%) and income (by 28 USD PPP, or 15%), we also find broader improvements in
savings, assets, employment, self-employment, food security, mental health, life satisfaction, aspira-
tions, women’s agency, and empowerment. Third, we attempt to draw inferences about the importance
of specific components. Programs with large transfers (at least 400 USD PPP) have larger treatment
effects. However, an important nuance is that they do not have larger effect per unit of cost. More
broadly, more expensive programs generate larger treatment effects, but lower cost programs tend to
be more cost-effective. Aside from larger transfers, the data do not tell a consistent pattern whereby
any other component stands out as either necessary or irrelevant.
Finally, we examine impacts for programs implemented more recently: average treatment effects,
cost-effectiveness, and benefit-cost ratios are all higher for programs in the past ten years, relative to
the first ten years when Graduation programs were implemented. Specifically, for example, using the
treatment effect persistence observed from our cross-study analysis, the benefit-cost ratio increases
from 2.89 for programs implemented through 2015 to 5.39 for programs implemented since 2016. This
contrasts with a common expectation in policy evaluation that effects attenuate as programs move from
initial pilots to wider implementation (Allcott, 2015; Al-Ubaydli et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 2017; List,
2022). We compare these patterns to two other types of interventions to assess hypotheses for this
trend: unconditional cash transfers (which acts as a placebo, on the premise that cash is less sensitive to
implementation fidelity but similarly prone to various manifestations of publication bias) and financial
education (which acts as a robustness test, for the opposite premise in terms of potential sensitivity
to implementation quality). We find a flat trend for unconditional cash transfers, but a similarly
upward trend for financial education impact on behavior change. We discuss possible mechanisms but
see this primarily as evidence for improved productivity via operational efficiency (although recognize
that this comparison to other sectors is not definitive). More broadly, this pattern also builds on the
productivity growth and knowledge spillovers literature, i.e., how diffusion of knowledge and practices
across producers can drive productivity gains (Bloom et al., 2013; Crespi et al., 2008).
1More recently, Baseler et al. (2026) focuses on economic and psychological spillover effects, including an examination
of important methodological questions regarding the method and public or private nature of the randomization that
determined program participation.
2The exception is for the benefit-cost analysis, when we compare our results to a re-analysis of 114 unconditional
cash transfer studies in Crosta et al. (2026).
3
2 Study Sample and Data
2.1 Study Search and Inclusion Criteria
We built the study sample through a staged screening process, summarized in Figure A.1. The initial
search used the terms graduation, livelihoods and multifaceted, together with randomized, evaluation,
poverty or low-income in Google Scholar, EconLit, and the AEA RCT Registry. 3 The search yielded
3,391 database records, which we cross-checked for exclusion errors against 115 studies from the PEI
State of Economic Inclusion Report evidence database (Andrews et al., 2021). After removing duplica-
tions, the search produced 2,604 unique candidate records. We then applied an initial relevance screen,
retaining 306 semi-finalist studies for detailed eligibility review. The large difference between these two
steps is due to the search terms (especially ”graduation”) picking up many studies on education that
are not relevant to poverty graduation programs. We then assessed whether each intervention satisfied
our graduation program definition of including at least three of five core components: a lump-sum
transfer, a stream of smaller transfers for consumption support, savings support, curriculum-based
training, and coaching or follow-up support. 4
Specifically, each study we include meets the following criteria:
1. The study is a randomized controlled trial.
2. The comparison arm received no intervention, a placebo, or business-as-usual services (such as
small regular transfers for consumption support).
3. The intervention was administered in a low- or middle-income country (as defined by World Bank
classification in August 2025).
At the level of the treatment arm, we use the following inclusion criteria:
1. The treatment arm administered at least three of the following five eligible treatment components:
(a) Consumption support
(b) Savings support (access or encouragement)
(c) Asset or lump sum cash transfer
(d) Skills training
(e) Coaching
2. The study reports results on any of the following outcomes: consumption, income, assets, employ-
ment, savings, food security, mental health, life satisfaction, aspirations, or female empowerment.
3Specifically, a June 2024 EconLit search used("graduation" OR "livelihood" OR "multifacet*") AND
("randomized" AND "evaluation") AND ("poverty" OR "low income") NOT "teacher", with related terms and all
years enabled.
4In September 2026, we added 8 studies that had been issued since our initial search and met the search criteria,
with the objective of ensuring that the results remained up to date.
4
Our inclusion criteria imply that we focus on multifaceted graduation and economic inclusion
interventions. We do not include simple “cash-plus” programs that administer a cash transfer and
only one additional treatment component (such as training). We note that some recent government-
led programs layer multifaceted interventions on top of public works programs. In this case, workfare
replaces regular cash transfers for consumption support. We do not include these programs unless they
independently meet the three-component criterion. This is because the number of studies is limited at
the time of writing, and public works imply different types of labor shifts and opportunity costs than
regular consumption support.
2.2 Sample Description
The final analysis sample draws on 49 study records from 41 publications, reports, and working pa-
pers, covering 40 unique randomizations. Across these records, we observe 81 reported treatment
variations and 123 treatment-variation-wave observations; consolidating repeated reports of the same
intervention lineage yields 68 unique treatment arms and 109 canonical treatment-arm-wave observa-
tions. Figure 1 summarizes the final analysis sample. 5 Our sample includes programs evaluated in
26 countries. Coverage is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, but it spans South Asia, Southeast
Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. About a quarter of the studies occurred in fragile or post-
conflict settings (specifically: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Chad, the Democratic Republic of Congo,
Niger, South Sudan, Uganda (with refugees from the DRC), and the Republic of Yemen).
Appendix Table A.1 reports component support and outcome sample sizes. In terms of compo-
nents, all treatment arms include training, and a majority includes an asset or lump-sum transfer,
coaching, and/or savings support. Despite these high-level similarities, the component details vary
across treatment arms. The value of lump-sum transfers varies sharply across treatment arms: some
variants omit a productive transfer entirely, while others provide transfers worth more than USD 1,000
in 2020 PPP terms (Data Appendix Table 2). Program cost and duration also vary meaningfully
throughout the sample. Income, consumption, and assets are all reported for a majority of treatment
arms, with coverage falling sharply for other outcomes, as we discuss next.
2.3 Data Extraction
2.3.1 DEVIDENCE Ecosystem for Data Extraction and Quality Control
We extracted treatment effects from published papers and appendices using the DEVIDENCE ex-
traction workflow from the Global Poverty Research lab at Northwestern University. For each study,
the extraction instrument recorded study metadata, publication and appendix links, treatment-control
comparisons, survey waves, units of randomization and analysis, treatment and control sample sizes,
treatment components, outcome labels, units, transformations, baseline values, endline values, and
5Data Appendix Table 1 lists all the included studies and references. Data Appendix Table 2 provides details on the
program components for each unique treatment arm.
5
reported treatment-effect estimates. We use reported estimates rather than re-estimating effects from
microdata.
When multiple estimates were available, we prioritized estimates that were disaggregated by treat-
ment arm and survey round. Within each arm-wave cell, we selected the measure with the highest
control group mean when there were multiple measures of monetary and non-index outcomes; for
indexed or standardized outcomes, we used the broadest measure possible. For example, the highest-
control-mean selection criterion led us to prioritize total household consumption over food consumption
alone and total household income over income from a single activity.
2.3.2 Key Outcome V ariables
We report 12 outcomes grouped into consumption, income, food security, savings, assets, employment,
psychological well-being, and female empowerment.
Consumption
Monthly household consumptioncaptures household-level consumption or total expenditure. If not
available at the household level, we scale per-capita consumption linearly by household size. If total
consumption is not available, we use the consumption or expenditure category with the next-largest
control group mean.
Income
Monthly household incomecaptures household-level income or earnings, and total revenue for busi-
nesses. Similarly to consumption, if household-level measures are not available, we proxy by per-capita
income adjusted for household size. If no aggregate measure of total income is available, we use the
income, earnings, or category with the next-largest control group mean.
F ood Security
Food securitycaptures study-reported food security scores, indices, and related indicators, coded so
that higher values indicate greater food security. The included studies use both established instruments—
including the Food Consumption Score (FCS), Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES), Household
Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS), and Household Hunger Scale (HHS)—and author-designed in-
dices based on experiences such as insufficient food, meal skipping, reduced portions, or going an entire
day without eating. We prioritize author-reported standardized indices where available and harmonize
the direction of all included measures.
Savings
Savings stockprioritizes savings balances or stocks where available. When no stock measure is re-
ported, we use savings flows, such as deposits over the month preceding follow-up.
6
Non-Financial Assets
Total assetspicks up measures of the total stock of household assets. If not available, we use the asset
category with the next-largest control group mean.
Employment
Any work reportedcaptures whether households report any form of work. We use this as the reported
employment outcome because activity type and work-intensity measures are less comparable across
studies. We note that studies do not consistently report engagement across all forms of work (in ei-
ther wage or self-employment, on or off-farm).Self-employment/Business operationcaptures whether
households report self-employment in off-farm income-generating activities or business operation.
Psychological W ell-Being
Mental healthcaptures mental health and psychological well-being indices, such as the Kessler mental
health score. If no standard index is reported, we use author-designed scores. In the absence of any
general index, we prioritize depression scores and indices. If none of the above are available, we use
single mental health symptoms or perceived stress scores. In 6 of the 18 studies contributing to the
mental health outcome, the selected measure is a narrower symptom, stress, or psychological-distress
scale rather than a broad mental health index.Satisfaction and happinesscomprises simple, one-item
life satisfaction and perceived happiness measures.Aspirations and expectationsis comprised mostly
of measures of general, educational, or child-related aspirations or general measures of future expec-
tations. If neither is available, we proxy with measures of optimism and whether respondents expect
life to improve. In three studies contributing to aspirations and expectations, the selected measure is
a proxy based on optimism, hopelessness, or whether respondents expect life to improve.
Empowerment
To capture notions of women’s empowerment, we use agency and general empowerment indices.
Agencyis a measure of household-level decision-making power and mostly picks up on indices about
women’s say in resource allocation. If no index is reported, we proxy by simple one-item measures
of power in household resource allocation and decision-making.General empowermentis strictly a
measure of general women’s or partner’s empowerment or disempowerment indices.
2.4 Costs Data
Of the 68 unique treatment arms in our sample, 48 provide intervention cost estimates, which for
descriptive reporting we express in constant 2020 market-exchange-rate USD per household, using
reported nominal costs where available and PPP-backconverted nominal equivalents otherwise.6 Across
these 48 arms in Data Appendix Table 3, estimated costs range from 102 USD to 3,090 USD per
6The quality of cost data varies widely, with some papers mentioning a unit cost without providing detailed informa-
tion and others providing detailed cost breakdowns.
7
participating household. The median cost is 445 USD, and the mean is 819 USD. One notable pattern

Abstract
This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market out-
comes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a
staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after convic-
tion to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly
earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry
as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are
more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.

1 Introduction
Imprisonment is often regarded as the most severe consequence of criminal activity. Yet,
many misdemeanours can bring about costs that extend beyond the courtroom. Drink-driving
1, a prevalent but often non-custodial offence, demonstrates this well: in the absence of
incarceration, convictions result in a criminal record, with lasting consequences on labour
market outcomes. This is most salient where background checks by employers are routine.
Several mechanisms may underpin these effects (Becker, 1968; Freeman, 1999). First,
the stigma associated with a criminal record can create substantial barriers to hiring and limit
access to employment opportunities (Uggen et al., 2014; Agan and Starr, 2017). Second, a
conviction may weaken attachment to the labour market by reducing incentives to seek or
retain employment (Visher et al., 2011; Sugie, 2018; Smith and Broege, 2020; Hjalmarsson
et al., 2024; Ramakers et al., 2025). Lastly, causality may also operate in the opposite direc-
tion: weaker labour market prospects may increase risky behaviours, such as heavy alcohol
consumption (MacDonald and Shields, 2001; Auld, 2005), thereby increasing the likelihood
of alcohol-related arrests and convictions.2 In this paper, we isolate and estimate the causal
effect of a drink-driving conviction on subsequent labour market outcomes in New Zealand.
We link administrative data from the Ministry of Justice court records, Inland Revenue
tax data, and the 2023 New Zealand Census to estimate the causal effect of a first-time drink-
driving conviction on employment and earnings. Our empirical strategy exploits variation
in the timing of conviction within a population of individuals who are all eventually con-
victed. We compare individuals before and after their first conviction with those convicted in
a later period using a staggered difference-in-differences design (Callaway and Sant’Anna,
2021). This avoids comparing offenders with non-offenders, since time-invariant differences
between the two groups could otherwise confound the relationship between conviction and
labour market outcomes. In our approach, both treatment and comparison groups are drawn
from the same population of eventual offenders, differing only in the timing of conviction.
We complement this design with an exact matching approach, comparing convicted individ-
uals to observationally similar members of the general public who do not receive a court
conviction during the sample period.

Drink-driving convictions in New Zealand are ideally suited for examining the informa-
tional consequences of criminal records. They are often non-custodial, involving fines or
temporary licence suspensions rather than imprisonment. Thus, our estimates abstract away
from incapacitation and human capital depreciation that occur during incarceration. Drink-
driving offences are also well suited to this design because severity is measured using breath
or blood alcohol readings, which provide an objective and continuous measure of the offence
that maps onto clear legal thresholds. This distinguishes drink-driving from many other mis-
demeanours, where severity may be more difficult to measure consistently (Sherman et al.,
2016). Furthermore, individuals may be uncertain about their precise alcohol concentration
at the time of driving (Love and Larue, 2025), meaning small measured differences in alcohol
concentration can translate into different legal outcomes. The availability of recorded alco-
hol readings allows us to construct a homogeneous analysis sample of first-time offenders
with readings in a narrow range at the lower end of the conviction distribution, all receiving
similar non-custodial penalties. This restriction is important: it allows us to focus on the ef-
fect of acquiring a criminal record among similar low-level offenders, avoiding comparisons
between individuals who differ substantially in offence severity or punishment.
Given the prevalence of such convictions, understanding their labour market conse-
quences is of clear importance. Linking the 2023 New Zealand Census to Ministry of Justice
court charge records, we find that 15.3% of men and 5.8% of women aged 30–55 have at least
one drink-driving conviction. Among those with a drink-driving conviction, 25.1% of men
and 43.9% of women have only a single recorded conviction. This suggests that drink-driving
convictions are relatively common among individuals with otherwise limited criminal his-
tories. These offences largely fall into the category ofsummary offences, the New Zealand
equivalent of misdemeanours, which are adjudicated without a jury and typically involve
non-custodial penalties. Internationally, comparable offence classes account for the majority
of criminal cases carried out in common-law jurisdictions.3 Despite their prevalence, lower-
level offences such as drink-driving have received relatively little attention in the literature,
which has instead focused disproportionately on incarceration and more serious crimes (for
an important exception, see Agan et al., 2023).

In contrast to an extensive literature on deterrence and road safety (Dee, 2001; Eisen-
berg, 2003; Albalate, 2008; Francesconi and James, 2021; Portillo et al., 2024; Ramasco,
2026), a small body of non-economic research on the consequences of drink-driving con-
victions documents negligible labour market impacts. Early studies have focused on the ef-
fects of licence suspension or revocation on employment outcomes. Wells-Parker and Cosby
(1988) used telephone surveys to compare 416 suspended and non-suspended DUI (driving
under the influence) offenders in Mississippi, United State and found limited evidence of
an effect on employment.4 Similarly, Knoebel and Ross (1997) surveyed 579 first-time and
233 repeat-DUI offenders across several US jurisdictions with differing licence revocation
regimes and reported minimal impacts on job status and income. The reliance on small,
self-reported survey data, however, limits the credibility of the estimates in these studies.
More recent work has used administrative data to examine broader economic outcomes
following drink-driving convictions. Using Finnish register data, Oksanen et al. (2015) show
that individuals are more likely to experience debt problems, divorce, and face an income
loss of approximately 20%, three years following their first offence. While this study ex-
ploits within-individual variation over time, it remains largely descriptive, lacking a formal
identification strategy and failing to account for pre-existing trends.
Our study also contributes to a growing economic literature examining how criminal
justice contact affects labour market outcomes through the information conveyed by a crim-
inal record itself (Finlay, 2009; Agan and Starr, 2017). A key finding in this literature is
that employers respond to information about criminal history, though effects are often het-
erogeneous and context-dependent. Evidence from field experiments shows that criminal
records reduce callback rates for job applicants. Concurrently, policies that restrict access
to information, such as “Ban-the-Box”, can alter employer screening in ways that generate
unintended consequences, including increased statistical discrimination against minority ap-
plicants (Agan and Starr, 2018). Subsequent research has shown considerable heterogeneity
in Ban-the-Box employment effects across data sources, institutional settings, and popula-
tion subgroups, yielding inconclusive evidence on aggregate employment impacts (Craigie,
2020; Doleac and Hansen, 2020; Shoag and Veuger, 2021; Rose, 2021; Burton and Wasser,
2025).
Related evidence from “clean slate” and record-remediation reforms, which conceal,
clear or reduce the severity of criminal records after a period without reoffending, also
points to modest earnings gains among the employed. However, the evidence on overall

The broader economic literature on criminal justice contact primarily focuses on incar-

as random judge assignment or sentencing thresholds, to estimate causal effects on employ-

strong pre-arrest labour market attachment (Mueller-Smith, 2015). 6 Pre-trial detention re-

2018), with similar evidence from Chile showing that pre-trial detention lowers formal em-

istrative datasets suggests a substantial share of observed earnings losses associated with
incarceration reflects incapacitation and weak pre-existing labour market attachment, rather
than long-run scarring, once time spent incarcerated is accounted for (Garin et al., 2025).
This literature is important but is less directly relevant to settings such as ours, where the
offence does not typically result in imprisonment.
This paper makes three contributions. First, it provides the first causal evidence on the
impact of drink-driving convictions on labour market outcomes, focusing on employment
and earnings rather than road safety or recidivism. We identify the economic consequences
of a criminal conviction by examining non-custodial drink-driving offences, exploiting new
linked administrative data that combine detailed court records, including recorded breath
alcohol levels, with earnings data. This setting allows us to abstract from imprisonment
and variation in sentencing severity, and to trace labour market trajectories before and after
conviction.
Second, we implement an identification strategy based on variation in the timing of in-
dividuals’ first drink-driving conviction. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design

persist beyond the typical six-month licence suspension period, suggesting that short-term
driving restrictions are unlikely to explain the results. We capture the essential elements of
our findings in a simple model of employer screening in a frictional labour market, which we
present in the penultimate section. This framework shows that convictions reduce perceived

First, alcohol concentration is measured using standardised breath or blood tests, generating

Enforcement relies on widespread roadside checks, with police authorised to stop drivers

5 Conclusion
In this paper we find that decreased employment following a drink-driving conviction is
primarily driven by a lower likelihood of entering employment. This indicates that such a
conviction is negatively updated by employers and operates as a barrier to job access. By
contrast, for individuals already employed, we find only small effects on job retention and
labour income, suggesting that the main margin of adjustment is labour market entry rather
than within-job outcomes.
Heterogeneity analysis reveals systematic differences in labour market responses by eth-
nicity and gender. Non-Europeans experience larger declines in employment and earnings
than Europeans. This difference is driven by both lower entry into employment and higher
exit rates. While these patterns are not statistically distinguishable, they are suggestive of
heterogeneous penalties that may reflect differences in how misdemeanor convictions are
processed in employer screening and hiring decisions. Men and women experience compa-
rable overall employment declines, but the underlying margins differ. Reduced entry is the
primary channel for men. For women both reduced entry and increased exit contribute.
These empirical patterns are consistent with the mechanism emphasised in our concep-
tual framework, in which a misdemeanor conviction lowers expected match value. It reduces
30
the probability that a match is formed in a frictional labour market. Given that a convic-
tion primarily affects employers’ hiring decisions rather than the productivity of incumbent
workers, the model predicts that employment entry should be the key adjustment margin,
with comparatively smaller effects on separations and wages.
Policy implications follow directly from this mechanism. Since the main cost of a drink-
driving conviction operates through reduced employment entry, with disproportionate effects
for non-European individuals and, through higher exit rates, for women, these findings point
to several areas where further research and policy evaluation may be warranted.
First, examining whether a clearer distinction between low-level and more serious crim-
inal offending in DUI enforcement—through non-conviction or diversionary pathways for
borderline misdemeanor cases—affects labour market outcomes would be valuable. Al-
though current thresholds already differentiate sanctions by alcohol levels in most countries,
future research could investigate whether a greater emphasis on non-conviction resolutions
where public safety risk is limited reduces employment penalties while maintaining deter-
rence. This possibility aligns with recent evidence finding that avoiding formal prosecution
can mitigate re-offending and prevent longer-term harms (Agan et al., 2023). However, our
findings suggest that such approaches alone would likely be insufficient to address the full
scope of employment barriers.
Second, examining modifications to existing Clean Slate schemes that could allow el-
igible individuals to withhold low-level convictions from employers may be particularly
relevant for minor traffic offences. Our results suggest that the main effects arise through
reduced re-entry into employment rather than lower earnings among incumbent workers,
suggesting that shorter waiting periods or fewer exceptions may help reduce the long-term
employment consequences of these convictions.
Third, fair-chance hiring approaches that limit initial access to criminal record infor-
mation during hiring may affect employment opportunities for individuals with low-level
criminal records. However, existing research suggests that limiting access to criminal-record
information can also encourage employers to rely more heavily on other observable char-
acteristics when making hiring decisions. Alternative approaches such as targeted hiring
incentives or time-limited record disclosure may therefore complement efforts to reduce the
consequences of prosecution.
More broadly, the evidence from this study indicates that even relatively minor misde-
meanor convictions can generate persistent labour-market effects through employer screen-

The French government is ruling out “nothing” in responding to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators that Paris has blamed on Iran, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Tuesday, AFP reported.
Barrot told Franceinfo that Iran’s ambassador will be summoned and that Paris will seek European sanctions against the Islamic regime. He said his government will take all measures “that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” including “those we may not disclose publicly.”
The goal, he said, is “to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again.”
On Monday, France accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of carrying out the attack last month, which made fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heat up. Millions of euros’ worth of food spoiled, and fires broke out in some stores.
Barrot called the attack “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression.”
Media reports have suggested similar cyberattacks may also have hit stores in other European countries.
Les 11 et 12 octobre, près de 700 sites de distribution ont été touchés par une campagne cyber d'une ampleur et d’une agressivité inédites.

France summoned Iran’s ambassador, accusing Tehran of a cyberattack disabling refrigerators in supermarkets, with Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot warning of potential cyber countermeasures.
Officials claimed Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind the October attacks affecting refrigeration systems across France.
The Iranian foreign ministry called these accusations “baseless and hostile.”
France’s Foreign Ministry confirmed the ambassador’s summoning took place on Tuesday.
Cyber response
Barrot indicated France might pursue EU sanctions, describing the attack as unprecedented.
He suggested undisclosed actions may follow.
France will take proportional measures deemed necessary to prevent future attacks and penalize responsible parties.
Barrot highlighted France’s cyberdefence options available to authorities.
The supermarket cyberattacks were among the most disruptive since the Iran conflict began, alongside attacks on the Los Angeles transit system and U.S. water plants.
Iran routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks.
Paris and Tehran relations have been tense due to Iran’s nuclear and missile programs, regional activities, and the detention of French nationals.
Relations briefly improved but soured again after diplomatic expulsions over the summer.
French officials cite Tehran’s hostility over France’s support for Iranian civil society.

France summoned Iran's ambassador on Tuesday over an alleged cyberattack that disrupted refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets across the country, with foreign minister Jean-Noel Barrot warning that Paris could retaliate with cyber measures of its own.
French officials on Monday accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of orchestrating the attacks, which affected commercial refrigeration systems across France in October, according to Reuters.
The French foreign ministry reportedly said the Iranian ambassador, whose summoning had been announced a day earlier by Barrot, was called in on Tuesday morning.

Speaking to France Info television, as cited by Reuters, Barrot called the incident an "attack of unprecedented scale and aggression" on French soil and said Paris would push for EU sanctions against Tehran in response.
He said there could be further action that would not be disclosed.
"We will take whatever measures are necessary, including some that we will not discuss publicly, if we judge them proportionate and necessary to deter any new attacks and punish those responsible for this unacceptable aggression," Barrot said and added France's cyberdefence doctrine provided authorities with a range of options.
According to AFP, the cyberattacks targeted 700 sites, with hackers gaining control of cooling systems through web interfaces to trigger "abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles". They also disabled sensor alerts designed to warn operators when temperatures crossed a specified threshold.

Similar incidents have since been reported in other European countries.
On November 2, stores in at least nine other European countries were hit by a suspected cyberattack on their freezer systems.

Tensions have also been fuelled by French allegations that Iran has spread misinformation linked to protests that have rocked France over the past month.
Iran's mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment on Monday, said Reuters.
A cyber unit linked to IRGC behind the cyberattacks?
Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that an investigation had been opened into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), over the attacks, according to AFP. Her office has also sought international arrest warrants against two officials associated with the unit.
Beccuau described Shahid Kaveh as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Centre of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-CEC)".
France's Centre for Coordination of Cyber Crises, which brings together security agencies, including intelligence services, said the unit conducts large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for sabotage. OFAC sanctions 45 more Prince Group targets as scam-compound enforcement scales into the billions
OFAC sanctioned 45 targets allegedly tied to Cambodia's Prince Group as new figures show scam compounds generated $12.7 billion in suspect activity.
The U.S. Treasury sanctioned 45 more targets on November 5, 2026 in its sustained campaign against Cambodia’s Prince Group, a conglomerate the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated a transnational criminal organization, and the numbers behind that campaign now run into the tens of billions of dollars.
Treasury said the Office of Foreign Assets Control designated four individuals and 41 entities it accuses of helping Prince Group executives conceal assets and launder the proceeds of crypto investment scams and romance scams run from Southeast Asian compounds. Treasury says those compounds rely on trafficked and coerced workers. Prince Group has denied the allegations.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the announcement that cyber scam syndicates “continue to steal billions of dollars from American victims while relying on sophisticated international business networks to launder their illicit proceeds.”
The enforcement wave keeps growing
The scale of the alleged fraud economy puts the Prince Group case in a different league from ordinary crypto enforcement. In September, Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) tied roughly $12.7 billion of reported transactions to suspected crypto investment fraud, mostly connected to Southeast Asian compounds. A July estimate from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) put 2025 victim losses to these operations at $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion, counting East and Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, with people from at least 80 countries held in the compounds.
The November 5 action was coordinated with the FBI and the Justice Department’s Scam Center Strike Force, which Treasury says has reported $580 million in crypto seizures and freezes, along with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Alaska and authorities in the British Virgin Islands and the UK. Washington is also pursuing forfeiture of roughly $14 billion in Bitcoin linked to the group, and UK authorities have frozen the London penthouse of alleged group finance chief Thet Li.
The designations block the targeted persons’ U.S. property and interests, requiring reports to OFAC, and any entity owned 50% or more by a blocked person is blocked as well. Treasury says violations can bring civil or criminal penalties, with civil penalties possible on a strict liability basis.
Striking at the corporate plumbing
The new names are the third U.S. sanctions tranche against Prince Group-linked actors in about 13 months, after designations in October 2025 and June 2026. Among the individuals Treasury named are Qiu Yong, whom Treasury says controls a web of British Virgin Islands and Hong Kong companies on the group’s behalf, and Zhao Mengyao, whom Treasury describes as Qiu’s personal assistant and a co-director of several Hong Kong companies he ultimately controls. Treasury also says the list includes He Yujing, the wife of Prince Group executive Chen Bo, to whom Chen transferred ownership of his Tokyo mansion after the October 2025 sanctions, and Visal Pang, who Treasury says controls 11 Cambodian companies. Chen Bo received his own U.S. designation on June 23, 2026.
Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi was arrested in Cambodia in January and extradited to China, leaving the designations aimed at the nominees, shells and administrators Treasury says are still holding the structure together. The group’s Prince Bank was placed into liquidation and Cambodia revoked Chen’s citizenship. Whether any of the 41 newly designated entities hold funds on exchanges or DeFi protocols that will now freeze them is not addressed in Treasury’s announcement.

a178.texte:
L’ESSENTIEL
- Une étude internationale désigne l’Europe comme le berceau probable des chauves-souris, il y a plus de 56 millions d’années.
- Les génomes de 103 espèces actuelles, croisés avec des fossiles, permettent de reconstituer la parenté et les déplacements de ces mammifères.
- Un fossile découvert en France étaye l’hypothèse d’une origine ancienne du sonar, sans résoudre l’ordre d’apparition du vol et de l’écholocalisation.
Depuis des décennies, les scientifiques débattent du lieu d’origine des chauves-souris. Une étude récemment publiée dans la revue Nature apporte de nouveaux éléments pour répondre à cette question. Ces travaux internationaux, qui combinent ADN et fossiles, désignent l’Europe comme leur berceau probable.
Jusqu’ici, la difficulté tenait à une différence avec les oiseaux, dont les nombreux fossiles retracent remarquablement la transition du dinosaure au « poulet » : les fossiles de chauves-souris que l’on découvre ressemblent déjà, de façon saisissante, à des « chauves-souris » presque entièrement formées.
Ce que l’on savait des premières chauves-souris
Les chauves-souris sont les seuls mammifères capables de vol actif. Des reconstitutions antérieures situaient leur berceau aux États-Unis, en Afrique ou en Asie, les réponses variant selon les jeux de données et les modèles utilisés. Les plus anciens squelettes de chauves-souris connus, découverts dans le Wyoming, aux États-Unis, remontent à environ 52 millions d’années, au début de l’Éocène. Leurs doigts allongés, qui soutenaient les ailes, montrent que ces animaux pouvaient déjà voler.
Toutefois, le lieu où l’on trouve les plus anciens fossiles connus ne révèle pas nécessairement où un groupe est apparu au cours de l’évolution. Ces fossiles fournissent néanmoins des indices importants sur l’anatomie, les liens de parenté et la répartition des premières chauves-souris. Ce qui manque, c’est une succession de fossiles retraçant la transition entre des ancêtres incapables de voler et les premières chauves-souris volantes.
La plupart des chauves-souris utilisent l’écholocalisation, une forme de sonar qui consiste à émettre des sons puis à se servir des échos renvoyés pour s’orienter et trouver de la nourriture. Outre la question de leur lieu d’origine, les scientifiques débattent de la façon dont le vol et l’écholocalisation sont apparus au cours de l’évolution. Lequel est apparu en premier, ou sont-ils apparus ensemble ?
Une étude de 2008 sur l’espèce fossile de chauve-souris Onychonycteris étayait l’hypothèse d’une apparition du vol en premier. Ses ailes indiquaient qu’elle pouvait voler, tandis que l’anatomie de ses oreilles suggérait qu’elle ne pratiquait pas l’écholocalisation. Toutefois, une étude de 2010, comparant l’anatomie d’Onychonycteris à celle de chauves-souris actuelles, a remis en cause cette interprétation.
Le vol a permis aux chauves-souris d’atteindre de nouvelles régions, tandis que l’écholocalisation leur a donné un moyen de s’orienter et de trouver de la nourriture dans l’obscurité. Un fossile interprété comme celui d’une chauve-souris capable de voler mais dépourvue d’écholocalisation pourrait correspondre à différents scénarios évolutifs. Sa lignée pourrait s’être séparée des autres avant l’apparition de l’écholocalisation, ou ses ancêtres pourraient avoir possédé cette faculté puis l’avoir perdue.
En combinant les données sur l’anatomie des fossiles et l’ADN de chauves-souris actuelles, les chercheurs peuvent situer cet animal parmi les espèces qui lui sont apparentées et évaluer ces possibilités. Même un fossile présentant des indices de ces deux capacités ne suffirait pas, à lui seul, à établir laquelle est apparue en premier, ni si elles sont apparues ensemble.
Cette capacité à se disperser complique aussi la recherche du berceau des chauves-souris. Les plus anciens fossiles connus pourraient appartenir à des populations qui s’étaient déjà propagées vers d’autres régions. Les scientifiques doivent croiser l’arbre généalogique des chauves-souris avec les données indiquant quand et où vivaient ses différentes branches.
Ce que change la nouvelle étude
L’étude récente marque une étape importante pour Bat1K, un projet international visant à produire des génomes de haute qualité pour toutes les espèces actuelles de chauves-souris. Un génome est l’ensemble des instructions génétiques d’un organisme. En comparant les génomes à la lumière des données fossiles, les chercheurs obtiennent bien davantage d’indices sur l’ascendance commune qu’avec des analyses fondées sur quelques gènes seulement, comme c’était le cas dans les travaux antérieurs.
Pour cette étude, les chercheurs ont analysé les génomes de 103 espèces de chauves-souris représentant les 21 familles actuelles. L’étude a aussi rassemblé des données anatomiques sur 65 espèces, dont 44 éteintes. Des scientifiques avaient déjà combiné des données moléculaires et fossiles. Ce qui distingue cette étude, c’est l’ampleur des données, la qualité des génomes et la recherche des raisons pour lesquelles différents segments d’ADN suggèrent parfois des liens de parenté différents entre groupes de chauves-souris.
La nouvelle analyse situe l’origine des chauves-souris en Europe, à la fin du Paléocène, une époque géologique, il y a plus de 56 millions d’années. Selon cette reconstitution, leurs descendants se sont propagés en Afrique, puis vers d’autres continents à mesure que les grands groupes de chauves-souris se diversifiaient. Cette conclusion repose sur une reconstitution des aires de répartition ancestrales à partir de l’arbre évolutif, des fossiles et de modèles qui prennent en compte les déplacements des continents et la dispersion des animaux. Dans cette analyse, de solides éléments étayaient l’hypothèse européenne.
Cette étude apporte aussi de nouveaux résultats sur l’origine de l’écholocalisation en établissant un lien entre les chauves-souris actuelles et Vielasia, une chauve-souris éteinte découverte en France. Un crâne fossile vieux de 50 millions d’années, décrit en 2023, présentait dans l’oreille interne des caractéristiques indiquant que cet animal pouvait utiliser une forme de sonar similaire à celle des chauves-souris actuelles pratiquant l’écholocalisation. La nouvelle étude situe Vielasia parmi les premiers groupes à s’être séparés, dans l’arbre évolutif, d’un ancêtre commun aux chauves-souris, ce qui renforce les indices d’une écholocalisation utilisant le larynx antérieure à la diversification des groupes actuels. Ces résultats étayent l’hypothèse d’une origine ancienne du sonar, sans résoudre la question de l’ordre précis d’apparition du vol et de l’écholocalisation.
Aujourd’hui, la diversité des chauves-souris est la plus grande sous les tropiques, mais l’Europe où elles seraient apparues était bien différente du continent que nous connaissons. À la fin du Paléocène, certaines régions d’Europe abritaient des forêts chaudes et subtropicales. Par périodes, des liaisons terrestres passant par le Groenland reliaient l’Europe à l’Amérique du Nord, permettant aux mammifères de circuler entre des régions aujourd’hui séparées par l’océan. Pour se représenter les débuts des chauves-souris, il faut imaginer ces forêts anciennes sur une carte où les voies de passage et les barrières étaient très différentes de celles d’aujourd’hui.

a165.texte:
Introduction
At its core, every cell is just a bubble of chemistry sealed inside a membrane. In modern cells, that chemistry is extraordinarily complex, orchestrating some 1 billion reactions per second. Likewise, its container, the lipid membrane, is built and maintained by elaborate biochemical mechanisms. But even the much simpler first cells would have needed a bubble too.
Without a physical boundary corralling molecules into a small space, whatever it was that turned into early life would have been too dispersed to assemble the complex systems that life requires, said Bruce Damer, an astrobiologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz. “You need a container before you can get the chemistry.”
To some researchers, the cell membrane seems so essential to life’s functions that they propose it as the origin of life. In this framework, known as the “lipid first” hypothesis, Earth transitioned from a mess of primordial chemistry to something recognizably alive because of those containers.
But many proponents of the lipid world go even further. They argue that the bubbles did more than hold chemistry. The bubbles themselves began to evolve.
Evolution requires a way for parents to pass traits to offspring. Modern life accomplishes this with complex biochemicals such as DNA and RNA, which can encode and copy information in their sequences. In the 1990s, researchers imagined a different possibility: What if a chemical system, rather than a molecule, could carry heritable information and become subject to evolution?
The idea begins with a puddle of water on the early Earth. The puddle is stocked with all kinds of small organic molecules, some homegrown and some delivered by dust and meteorites. Many of these molecules have a split personality. One end of them is drawn to water, or “hydrophilic.” The other is repelled by water in the same way that oil is. These “hydrophobic” ends will huddle together to hide from the water, while the hydrophilic ends will face outward. These behaviors cause the molecules to form a tiny sphere — a bubble.
The primordial puddle also has other molecules, simpler raw ingredients that can, under the correct circumstances, be turned into more of themselves. Here’s how that works: Imagine that a bubble contains two special molecules, molecule A and molecule B. Each of these molecules speeds up a chemical reaction that uses other ingredients in the puddle. Molecule A, in this case, speeds up chemical reactions that produce molecule B. After a while, the bubble fills up with B’s. These, in turn, may speed up the production of another kind of molecule.
Sometimes, there might be a puddle where B’s return the favor and make more A’s. The A’s make more B’s, then the B’s make more A’s. Each type keeps the other topped up in an endless loop. The bubble containing these A’s and B’s will grow, but the ratio of molecules will stay more or less steady.
In time, the bubble will split, and its molecules will be dealt out into its baby bubbles. Each of these may get some A’s and some B’s, and the symbiotic loop will keep running, building the parent’s compositional recipe more faithfully than chance alone would. Unlike with DNA, which is copied exactly, letter by letter, a proportion of molecules gets passed down to the next generation of bubbles.
But evolution needs more than heredity. It needs to allow for change. In our chemical soup, that possibility comes from a stray molecule C, which like a mutation tips a bubble into a different molecular loop. Faster-growing bubbles split more often and crowd out slower-growing bubbles, so the fast-moving descendants will make up a bigger and bigger share of the crowd. Slow recipes get squeezed out.
In 2000, Doron Lancet, a geneticist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, and Daniel Segrè, a computational biologist at Boston University, published the results of a computer model that explored whether these dynamics could lead to lifelike behavior. They found that bubbles can pass their compositions to their daughters, which vary and compete, fulfilling the requirements for natural selection. In their computer model, at least, the lipid-world idea passed its first test.
Which molecules could build these bubbles? In the original simulation, molecules A, B, and the rest would be different kinds of lipids. The team settled on lipids, the molecules that make up modern cell membranes, in part because they mirror the model’s required half-hydrophobic, half-hydrophilic nature. When lipids are dropped into water, they can assemble into double-layered sheets. Under the right conditions, the sheets close in on themselves, forming a sphere with a pocket of water trapped inside.
But in the 25 years since Lancet, Segrè, and their colleagues published the original lipid-world hypothesis, scientists have questioned whether the first compartments had to be made of lipids at all. Couldn’t other types of molecules have formed a container first? “There really isn’t a distinct lipid-world hypothesis anymore,” Damer said. Researchers have proposed that certain minerals, such as iron sulfides, could have formed the walls of a container, or that coacervates — liquidlike droplets where molecules gather and concentrate — could have acted as membrane-free vessels for early chemistry.
Damer and David Deamer, a Santa Cruz biochemist who worked with Lancet and Segrè on the original hypothesis, have stayed focused on lipids, but in a specific setting: hot-spring pools. They now study whether the repeated drying and refilling of such pools could have squeezed simple molecules between layers of lipids to develop increasingly complex systems. Damer views their more recent “hot spring hypothesis” as an extension of the lipid world.
Origins-of-life research is famously contentious, and scientists in the field debate the lipid world against other ideas about how life formed. “The idea of a lipid-only form of primitive life has never made sense to me,” said Jack Szostak, a Nobel Prize–winning biochemist at the University of Chicago. He cited the lack of experimental evidence that a lipid-based system can evolve. Plus, he said, how even simple lipids would have formed on the early Earth is “the least well-developed aspect of all of prebiotic chemistry.”
Another criticism strikes at the heart of the original computer simulation. A 2010 analysis suggested that the replication of compositional information from one generation to the next would be too inaccurate for natural selection to work.
None of these objections, though, is about whether early life needed a bubble. Even Szostak, who favors an RNA-based explanation for the origin of life, agrees on the point that the lipid-first camp cares about most — that compartments are necessary to keep related molecules together. Without them, he said, “Darwinian evolution could not operate.”
